findings.title: Match statistics are rolled back whenever the block actually happens.
findings.body: `should_block?` runs inside `User#valid?`, and ActiveRecord runs that inside the transaction that `user.save` opens. When the email is blocked, validation fails, `save` returns false and the transaction is rolled back. That rollback also undoes the `match_count`/`last_match_at` update made here. So for `:block` records, the counters never change during real signups. They only move for `:do_nothing` records or when `should_block?` is called on its own, as the spec does. Record the match outside the user's transaction (for example in a separate connection or job, or after the failed save in the controller), or move the check out of the model validation. I couldn't see whether `UsersController#create` uses `user.save`, but that is the usual path.

findings.title: Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive, so changing letter case gets past the block.
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` is an exact, case-sensitive match. If `bad@spammers.org` is blocked, signing up as `Bad@Spammers.org` is not matched, so the block is trivially bypassed. Nothing shown here downcases the email before validation. Normalize both sides: store the email lowercased and look it up with `where(email: email.downcase)` (or `lower(email)`). Ideally make the unique index case-insensitive as well.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count loses increments under concurrency.
findings.body: The count is loaded, incremented in Ruby and saved back. Two signups that check the same email at once both read N and write N+1, so a match is lost. Do the increment in the database instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`.
